newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia says U.S. worry holds up trade benefits.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia says U.S. worry holds up trade benefits.

text.p: Cambodian Minister of Commerce Cham Prasidh said on Tuesday that U.S. concern over political problems in Cambodia was holding up the nation's application for American trade benefits.

But despite recent political instability, Cambodia remained on track for entry into the World Trade Organisation (WTO) by the end of 1998, Prasidh told reporters at a seminar on the WTO and multilateral trade.

Cambodia won Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trade status from the United States last year. Now it is waiting for a decision on U.S. Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) trade status, which would allow it to export specified products to the United States duty-free.
Cham Prasidh said Cambodia's passage of a new labour law earlier this year should have made it eligible for GSP, but that politics were now getting in the way.

"It (the application) is stuck somewhere because there has been some concern that the situation might deteriorate in Cambodia, so some people are not willing at this stage to consider examining the possibility of providing GSP to Cambodia."
Cambodia's government has been largely paralysed since a March 30 grenade attack on an opposition rally that killed 19 people and injured more than 150.

Long-time tensions between the ruling coalition's two co-premiers, Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen, have worsened considerably since the attack, and the international community has expressed concern that Cambodian democracy is in danger.
The commerce minister said the Cambodian situation "was not as bad as three or four years ago," and urged the U.S. administration to put the GSP application on the fast track.
As for the WTO, Cham Prasidh said: "We are still hoping to (join) by the end of 1998."

Cambodia gained observer status in the world trade body in 1995, but full membership would provide needed "predictability for business people and fewer problems negotiating with other countries," he said.
